newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Six seek presidential nomination of S.Korea party.
newsitem.headline: Six seek presidential nomination of S.Korea party.

text.p: South Korea's troubled ruling party began balloting its delegates on Monday to elect its candidate for presidential elections in December.
More than 12,000 representatives of the New Korea Party filled a gymnastics stadium in Seoul in the first ever open race for a presidential nominee by the party.

President Kim Young-sam, who cannot seek re-election under the constitution, opened the meeting by urging party members to rally behind a candidate after mud-slinging and allegations of vote-buying during the past two weeks of campaigning.
"Let's melt down trivial emotional confrontations and conflicts in this furnace of compromise," said Kim, who is also the president of the party.
Political analysts said most worrying for the New Korea Party is the prospect of one of the contenders leaving the party to run alone in December elections to split the ruling camp ticket.

Kim, who has been reduced to a lame duck by bribery scandals and political blunders, has given up his earlier plan to act as a kingmaker. Former supreme court judge Lee Hoi-chang has been leading in most public polls among the New Korea Party's six presidential hopefuls but lacks the 50 percent support among party delegates needed to win nomination.
If no one secures 50 percent of votes cast, a second round of polls would be held later on Monday between the two top contenders.
Four contenders vowed overnight that they would unite against Lee Hoi-chang in the run-off vote to support whoever emerges as the runner-up among them.
"We have agreed to form an alliance against Mr Lee Hoi-chang," prosecutor-turned-lawmaker Lee Han-dong, one of the four, told reporters.

Governor Rhee In-je of Kyonggi Province which surrounds Seoul, Kim's long-time aide Kim Deog-ryong and ex-premier and legal scholar Lee Soo-sung also confirmed unity against Lee Hoi-chang, who built his reputation as "Mr Clean" as a supreme court judge.
The sixth presidential hopeful is former Seoul mayor Choe Byung-yul, who analysts said had little chance in the race.

President Kim has repeatedly said he will remain neutral in the nomination race but several members of his inner circle have openly campaigned against the former judge, who won prominence by challenging Kim's administration style.

Analysts said Kim loyalists would try to install Kim's protege Kim Deog-ryong in office to protect him after retirement. They noted that the alliance among the four contenders was engineered by Suh Chung-won, a member of President Kim's inner circle.

The opposition accuses the president of illegally using money from the scandal-ridden Hanbo Group to fund his presidential campaign in 1992 and of dipping into a slush fund amassed by his disgraced predecessor Roh Tae-woo.
Roh is now serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and human rights abuses.
The ruling party has been on the defensive since it provoked almost four weeks of labour strikes after ramming a controversial new labour law through parliament last December.
Several senior party figures are also serving jail terms for taking kickbacks from the Hanbo Group, whose steelmaking flagship collapsed in January, revealing a web of corruption.
